name: Amiloride

lead: Amiloride is a mild diuretic that is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk as a way to reduce fluid and facial puffiness.

It blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal kidney tubule, so sodium and water are excreted while potassium is retained. It is normally added to a thiazide diuretic for heart failure or high blood pressure. No study has examined it for facial puffiness or appearance.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, usually paired with a thiazide diuretic in medical use, where it also offsets potassium loss from the other drug.

The label's boxed warning says high potassium can be fatal if uncorrected, with roughly 10 percent incidence when used without another diuretic and higher risk with kidney disease, diabetes and older age. Minor nausea and abdominal symptoms are common. It is prescription-only.

chain: Mild diuretic removes sodium and water
angle.text: Amiloride is a mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics, and it is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk for a less puffy face. It blocks sodium channels in the kidney so sodium and water are excreted. No research addresses facial puffiness.

lead: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that directly blocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, producing a mild increase in sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium. It is used mainly alongside thiazide or other potassium-wasting diuretics in heart failure and hypertension.[1][2][3]

It is listed on the wiki under depuffing because it is a diuretic: by increasing sodium and water loss it reduces fluid, and some people who want a leaner or less puffy look are interested in diuretics for that reason. Amiloride is also on anti-doping lists as a masking agent, which is how it appears in bodybuilding-forum contexts.[4][5] No published trial has tested amiloride for facial puffiness or any appearance outcome.
Its US label carries a boxed warning on hyperkalemia, reported in about 10 percent of patients when amiloride is used without a potassium-wasting diuretic.[2]

paras: People interested in a leaner, less puffy look sometimes consider diuretics because less retained water can make the face and midsection appear sharper. Amiloride fits that thinking mechanistically: it blocks sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron so more sodium and water leave in the urine, while potassium is conserved.[1][6][5]

The effect is described as mild. Grokipedia states that amiloride's natriuretic and antihypertensive effects are weaker than those of thiazides, which is why it is used with other diuretics rather than alone.[1] In the physique world the drug is chiefly encountered on rule lists, since natural bodybuilding federations and sports leagues name amiloride among prohibited diuretics.[7][8]
Amiloride is a prescription drug. Clinicians prescribe it for blood pressure and fluid problems, and the label's warnings on potassium apply to everyone taking it.[2]

The US label indicates amiloride as adjunctive treatment with thiazide or other kaliuretic diuretics in congestive heart failure or hypertension, to restore normal potassium or prevent hypokalemia.[2] Grokipedia notes its diuretic and antihypertensive effects are weaker than those of thiazides, so it is used as an adjunct.[1] Wikipedia lists additional uses including Liddle phenotype, ascites and edema in cirrhosis, and off-label use to reduce urine volume in lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which a 2022 review also discusses.[3][4][9]

A 2025 randomised trial in South Korea enrolled 118 patients with resistant hypertension whose home systolic pressure stayed at or above 130 mm Hg on triple therapy and randomised them to spironolactone or amiloride to test non-inferiority on home systolic blood pressure at week 12.[10] Earlier controlled trials from 1968 examined amiloride in hypertensive patients and its effect on plasma potassium, and a 1986 trial studied hypokalemia in thiazide-treated hypertension.[11][12][13] None of these measured facial puffiness or physique appearance.

The epithelial sodium channel that amiloride blocks was cloned in 1994 and is made of three homologous subunits; it carries the rate-limiting step of sodium reabsorption in the distal renal tubule, colon, and some exocrine ducts and lung.[6] Gain-of-function mutations in the channel cause Liddle's syndrome, a heritable form of hypertension.[14] A 1987 review places potassium-sparing diuretics, including amiloride, in the late distal tubule to collecting duct, where blocking luminal sodium channels reduces sodium transport.[5] Amiloride has also been used as a research tool for ion transport.[15]

According to Wikipedia, onset is about two hours, peak diuresis occurs at 6 to 10 hours, the effect lasts about 24 hours and the elimination half-life is 6 to 9 hours; the drug is not metabolised by the liver.[4]

Amiloride is a pyrazinoylguanidine derivative with the molecular formula C6H8ClN7O.[1] Grokipedia reports that it is excreted largely unchanged, about half in urine and about 40 percent in feces, with a half-life of 6 to 9 hours.[1]

The label states that amiloride is usually well tolerated apart from hyperkalemia, which if uncorrected is potentially fatal and is more likely with renal impairment, diabetes and older age.[2] When used with a thiazide in patients without those complications, the label puts the hyperkalemia risk at about 1 to 2 percent.[2] Minor reactions such as nausea, abdominal pain and flatulence were reported in about 20 percent of patients, with frequency similar to hydrochlorothiazide groups.[2] Animal studies at high multiples of the human dose found no fetal harm, though the drug crossed the placenta.[2]

The label contraindicates amiloride in people with existing hyperkalemia, significant kidney impairment or hypersensitivity, and notes the added hyperkalemia risk in diabetes and older age.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that the drug is in the FDA pregnancy category B, based on animal studies without fetal harm and a lack of well-controlled human studies, and that its excretion in breast milk is uncertain.[1] Because its effects on potassium are the main safety concern, the label's boxed warning on hyperkalemia is the feature regulators highlight, and the risk is higher when amiloride is combined with other potassium-sparing agents.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that Merck Sharp & Dohme researchers discovered amiloride in the late 1960s in a screen for compounds that reversed mineralocorticoid effects, and that it was the only compound in the screen causing sodium excretion without potassium loss; the FDA approved it on October 5, 1981.[4] Clinical reports from 1968 describe early human trials.[11][12] In 1994 the amiloride-sensitive sodium channel subunits were cloned and Liddle's syndrome was linked to channel mutations.[6][14]

Amiloride is on the World Anti-Doping Agency list as a diuretic masking agent because diuresis can dilute other substances in urine; Wikipedia notes it appeared in about 3 percent of positive diuretic doping samples in 2008.[4] Natural bodybuilding federation rules and NFL banned-substance lists posted on T Nation name amiloride among prohibited diuretics.[7][8] These posts concern competition rules rather than endorsements of use.

No studies found on amiloride for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing. Registered trials concern resistant hypertension, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis and migraine aura, among others.[16][17] Published trials include the 2025 spironolactone-versus-amiloride comparison in resistant hypertension and a pharmacokinetic trial of intranasal amiloride in healthy volunteers.[10][18]

Other registered work includes a trial in resistant hypertension with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria, a study of the natriuretic response in relation to a genetic variant, a phase 2 trial in optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis, a migraine aura study and small studies in nephrotic syndrome, prehypertension and a nasal spray formulation.[16][17] Grokipedia describes the 2025 resistant-hypertension trial as showing noninferiority to spironolactone, with home systolic pressure reductions of about 13.6 mm Hg.[1][10]

lore.intro: Amiloride appears in bodybuilding-forum posts mainly as a banned masking-agent diuretic on federation and league lists.[7][8]

claims.claim: Prescription diuretics such as amiloride can be used to shed water for a leaner look.
Amiloride is a gentler diuretic than the thiazides or loop diuretics used in some physique circles.
